en: Homage to Tārā!

Here, in the case of a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), the pervasion consisting of negative concomitance (*vyatireka-ātmikā vyāptiḥ*), which implies the form of positive concomitance (*ākṣipta-anvaya-rūpiṇī*), is stated for the reason of existence (*sattva-hetu*).
(77.6) Whatever exists is momentary, just like a jar; and these entities under dispute exist. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
(77.8) First of all, its non-establishment is not possible;

for, in a subject (*dharmin*) cognized through the means of valid cognition—namely perception and inference—the probans intended by the word "existence," characterized as the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), is established by valid cognition.
(77.10) Nor is there [the fallacies of] contradiction or inconclusiveness.
Because pervasion is established by a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) consisting in the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) in the case of the opposite [of the probandum]:
that which lacks both succession and simultaneity does not possess the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*),
just like a rabbit's horn.
Since neither succession nor simultaneity exist for that which is non-momentary, this is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*).
First of all, this reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*),
because it is impossible for succession or simultaneity to exist in a non-momentary subject (*dharmin*).

For instance, if that which has reached another time were identical [to its prior state], it would be eternal. Yet, if such a thing were to possess succession or non-succession, there would necessarily be a difference between even two moments.
Since difference and non-difference are mutually contradictory, how could succession or non-succession be possible in a non-momentary entity?
If there is a difference between the two moments, then the application of succession or simultaneity [is untenable].

For if there were non-difference, since the entity would be potent in the very first moment, it would follow that it must produce even a future effect; in that case, how could there be any occasion for a different succession in the production of another effect?
Furthermore, it is not the case that a non-momentary entity, having performed its entire range of effects simultaneously, remains in a state of rest;
for since it would remain capable at subsequent moments as well, there would follow the undesirable consequence of it performing those effects again.
Therefore, "non-momentary" implies the absence of difference between earlier and later times.
The "conjunction of succession and non-succession" refers to the distinction between earlier and later times;
and between these two, there exists a contradiction characterized by their mutual exclusion.
Therefore, this reason—characterized by the absence of both succession and non-succession in a non-momentary subject—must not be said to be unestablished (*asiddha*).
This is precisely because there is a contradiction between being endowed with succession and non-succession on the one hand, and momentariness on the other;
nor is it contradictory [to the probandum],
because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*).
Nor is [the reason] inconclusive,
because the absence of succession and simultaneity is pervaded by the absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*).

For it has been established by that very means of valid cognition which is of the nature of direct perception— that since there are no other possible modes, causal efficiency, being of a positive nature, is pervaded by succession and simultaneity, which are themselves of a positive nature.
Therefore, it must be accepted that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the absence of succession and simultaneity by that very same absence of causal efficacy has been established.

For there exists no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) capable of establishing the pervasion of the absence of fire and so forth by the absence of smoke and so forth, apart from the means of valid cognition that establishes the pervasion of smoke and so forth by fire and so forth.
Consequently, this is the principle: whatever establishes the pervasion between two positive entities (*vidhi*) also establishes the pervasion between two absences (*abhāva*).

Because it is impossible to transcend [the pervasion], the absence of succession and non-succession is indeed pervaded by the absence of existence; thus, the reason is not inconclusive, and the non-perception of the pervader is faultless.

Therefore, this [reason]—by excluding existence from that which is non-momentary and thereby excluding its own pervaded [property, existence]—causes existence to rest in the momentary. Thus, the proof of momentary destruction through the reason of existence is also faultless.

(78.10) But surely, how can existence (*sattva*) be established as being necessarily connected to its own probandum (*svasādhya*) on the basis of the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*),
since this [reason] too is corrupted by many defects? For instance, it is certainly not a *prasaṅga* reason (*hetu*).

Because it is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), because it is not established merely by the opponent's admission, and because there is no reduction to the contrary (*viparyayaparyavasāna*).
If, on the other hand, it is independent,
then it is unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*),
because a non-momentary locus is impossible.
Or [it is invalid] because it is not recognized (*apratītatvāt*).
For recognition would have to occur either through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), or mere conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*).

In the first two cases, if [the subject] were to perform its function as an object characterized by being recognized by itself—either directly or through a causal chain—the primary reason (*maula-hetu*) would be "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*), and the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) would be "unestablished in its own nature" (*svarūpāsiddha*).

Because, in the case of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), one of the two— succession or simultaneity— necessarily occurs. However, in the final position [of non-momentariness], no cause whatsoever would be without a substratum,
since a subject (*dharmin*) established by mere conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*) is easily found everywhere.
Furthermore, that conceptual cognition must be either subsequent to perception, born from a logical mark,
or produced by a mental impression.
Whether the object is of a doubtful nature or non-existent;
in those first two cases, the existence of the non-momentary remains unimpeded.
How does a subverting proof apply?
(79.9) In the third case, however, there is not always a negation of the existence of non-momentary things;
for in the absence of the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by that [perception], recollection of it would be impossible.
In the fourth [reason], however, there is the fallacy of the reason (*hetudoṣa*) known as "having a doubtful substratum" (*sandigdhāśrayatva*).

Furthermore, in the fifth [reason], the non-existence of that object is not established by perception, because according to your own view, a non-momentary self is never perceived. Nor is its non-existence established by inference, because no probans (*liṅga*) concomitant with it is observed; thus, the fallacy of the unestablished substratum (*āśrayāsiddhi*) is first set forth.
In this way, the example as well must be refuted. Furthermore, this reason is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*),
because even for a permanent entity, purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) through both successive and simultaneous means is possible by depending on successive or simultaneous auxiliary causes.
Nor does the fault stated regarding the positions of succession and simultaneity follow;
for it is not contradictory that [a cause] produces successive effects by depending on successive auxiliary conditions.
And such is Śaṅkara’s concise intention:
For capacity (*sāmarthya*) is indeed the completeness of auxiliary factors (*sahakāri-sākalya*),
and incapacity (*asāmarthya*) is their deficiency (*vaikalya*).
And there is no impairment whatsoever of that which possesses these [capacities and incapacities] by their appearance or disappearance.
Since that [cause] is distinct from those two,
how can there be the consequence that it performs its function independently of its auxiliary causes?
This is also the summarized meaning of Trilocana’s position.
For it is the effect alone that depends upon auxiliary causes, not the cause of the production of the effect;
because capacity is of two kinds: innate and adventitious, which consists of another auxiliary cause.

Therefore, since even for a non-momentary entity, a variety of effects can arise sequentially due to a variety of sequential auxiliary causes, it is impossible to establish that entities are distinct at every moment.
Thus the Nyāyabhūṣaṇa also says:
"For at the time of producing the first effect, [the cause] possesses the nature of producing subsequent effects."
If it is argued that, therefore, one should perform all effects at the very first moment,
this is untenable because it contradicts one's own words— like saying, "My mother is barren.
For how could that which has the nature of producing a subsequent effect produce that effect at the outset?
In that case, it would not have the nature of performing that specific effect;
for that which has the nature of producing blue does not also produce yellow and so forth.
Vācaspati also recites this:
Now, this non-momentary entity produces its effect by means of its own nature (*svarūpa*).

Since that nature of it exists at the second moment just as it does at the third and subsequent moments, it should produce [the effect] then as well. Or, if it does not produce it then, it would not produce it at the third and subsequent moments either.
Because it remains in that same state; or, if it does not remain in that state, then that itself is its momentariness.
To this it is replied: It is true that it produces an effect by way of its own nature, but not by that very [nature] alone.
Since it is observed that an effect arises only from that [cause] when accompanied by auxiliary factors,

therefore, just like pervasion (*vyāpti*), the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) must be understood in one case through the exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), and in the other case through the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*).
In the same way, because there is agreement among worldly investigators, there is no occasion for the faults stated regarding the position that [causes] produce effects sequentially;
nor is there any room for the faults stated regarding the position of simultaneity for non-momentary things.

For those specific substances that have produced an effect possess an activity capable of producing a determined effect, which persists even while those substances continue to exist after the effect has been accomplished, since its purpose has already been fulfilled.
The causal totality is incomplete;
how then could that which has already been produced produce [anything]?
For the staff and other such factors are not by their very nature agents, such that they would perform an action starting from the moment of production.
Rather, they are those who enter into activity.
And it is not by virtue of this [activity] that they cease to be agents;
for they enter into activity precisely for the sake of fulfilling their status as agents by means of their own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Furthermore, there will be the absence of both succession and simultaneity, yet there is no absence of existence;
thus, this non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) has a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatireka*).
For it is not established that there is an absence of any other mode besides succession and simultaneity.

Because a specific negation has as its scope the permission of what remains [aside from the negated]. Furthermore, if another mode [of causal efficiency] were perceptible, there would be no absolute negation;

if it were imperceptible, however, there would be no certainty regarding its non-existence for things that are remote. Thus, the pervasion of the capacity for causal efficiency by either succession or simultaneity is not established.

Therefore, the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) also has a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatireka*). Furthermore, since succession and simultaneity—which possess the totality of perceptible and imperceptible auxiliary conditions—are entirely beyond the senses, existence (*sattva*), which is pervaded by them, is likewise imperceptible; thus, the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) cannot be established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Nor can [the object] be established through inference,
because there is no logical mark (liṅga) invariably concomitant with it.
Furthermore, it is a most excellent saying that the capacity for causal efficiency is pervaded by either succession or simultaneity.
If it is pervaded sequentially, how can it be [pervaded] non-sequentially?
Or if it is pervaded non-sequentially, then it is not [pervaded] sequentially.
By asserting that pervasion occurs through both sequence and non-sequence, one demonstrates the very absence of pervasion.
For it is not the case that fire is pervaded by the presence or absence of smoke;
therefore, the pervasion is inconclusive.
Furthermore, does this subverting argument establish the non-existence of non-momentary things?
Is it the exclusion of existence from that which is non-momentary? Or is it the necessary connection between existence and momentariness?
It is not the first alternative.
Because, according to the stated sequence, the reason suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*).
Nor is the second [alternative] possible;
for the meaning of the term "negative concomitance" (*vyatireka*) is the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) accompanied by the absence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*).
And if that [non-existence] were perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then it would be its cause; thus, existence (*sattva*) is an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*).
The non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*).
If, on the other hand, it is conceptualized (*vikalpyate*), then the conceptualization must be refuted by analyzing it into five ways according to the sequence previously stated.
(81.1) For this very reason, the third alternative is also not tenable; for as long as a distinction [between subject and predicate] is unestablished, a relation cannot be established.
(81.2) Furthermore, unlike the case of the bare ground, a non-momentary subject is not perceived here.

Furthermore, when there is a non-perception of intrinsic nature, the non-perception of the pervader cannot be subsumed under any perceptible object without first establishing that [object]. Moreover, if this [non-perception] were a property of non-existence, it would entail the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatva*) and mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*); if it were a property of existence, it would entail the fallacy of contradiction (*viruddhatva*).
Furthermore, if it possesses both natures, the reason is inconclusive; thus, it does not escape the three types of logical fallacy.

As for what was stated—that in the case of non-momentariness, causal efficiency is contradicted by [the impossibility of] successive or simultaneous action—there, one who seeks to establish that contradiction must also understand the contradictory counterpart.
This is because the establishment of contradiction is inseparable from the cognition of that [contrary];

as, for example, in the case of snow and fire, or of dependent and independent entities. Furthermore, the non-momentary entity, being perceived as a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), must indeed exist, because it is an object of cognition; for that which does not produce [cognition] cannot be an object of knowledge (*aprameya*).
(81.10) If it is argued that the establishment of contradiction is achieved through momentariness established by conventional consensus (*saṃvṛti*), [we reply:
even that which is established conventionally must be either real or conceptual.
(81.12) If it were real, how could it be non-existent?

And how is there a contradiction with the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*)? For that which performs causal efficiency is said to be real; otherwise, it would be merely conceptual (*kālpānika*).
In that regard, is the contradiction real or conceptual?
It is certainly not real.
Because it is a contradiction between two imagined [entities],
like the contradiction between a barren woman’s son [and something else];
or, alternatively, the contradiction itself is merely imagined.
"In that case, the exclusion of a sentient being is not ultimate, and thus the doctrine of momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) is rendered a mere empty gesture.
(81.17) This very series of objections was summarized by our teachers as follows:

(81.18) "It is neither eternal nor is it an object of cognition; therefore, the reason [adduced] suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhatā). Furthermore, one's own experience is undermined, and the concordant instance (sapakṣa) is also discarded."

"Emptiness is established through the absence of duality; yet non-existence is not [established] by existence, just as the establishment of contradiction with the eternal cannot be achieved by means of the non-existent, nor even by means of succession and so forth.

(From the *Kṣaṇabhaṅgādhyāya*, 81.23). To this it is replied: Here, even regarding a real entity (*vastu*), the conventional usage of subject (*dharmin*) and property (*dharma*) is observed, just as "cowness" is [observed] in a cow.
In a cloth there is whiteness; in a horse, movement—and so forth.

Even regarding non-entities (*avastu*), the conventional usage of subject (*dharmin*) and property (*dharma*) is observed, such as: the absence of sharpness in a rabbit’s horn, the absence of speakerhood in the son of a barren woman, the absence of fragrance in a sky-lotus, and so on.
In that regard, if one says that a non-entity lacks the status of a subject, does this mean that it lacks the status of a subject by virtue of being a property of an entity?
Or is it by means of a property that is not a real entity?
In the first case, there is the proving of what is already established;
in the second case, however, there is a contradiction with one's own words.
As the teachers have said:

(81.28) Is there here, regarding some property (*dharma*) in a non-entity (*avastu*), the conventional practice of negation and affirmation established by the mind, or not? If it exists somewhere, how can there not be so many refutations? If it does not exist at all, then the contradiction with one's own words is established. (82.1) The meaning is that, because the pervader—the state of being preceded by the acceptance of a non-entity as a subject (*dharmin*)—is absent, there follows the consequence that the refutation of the "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*) cannot be put forward.
For by the very same statement that negates the status of being a subject (*dharmitva*) for a non-entity,
one has already admitted the status of being a subject through that very property (*dharma*) which is the absence of the status of being a subject for a non-entity;
yet it is subsequently negated— this is clearly the work of a deity.

For thus, regarding the statement that "a non-entity lacks the status of being a subject," there are three possible positions: is the absence of the status of being a subject predicated of the non-entity itself, or elsewhere, or is it not predicated of anything at all?

(82.6) In the first case, there is no negation of the subject-status (*dharmitva*) of a non-entity, because the property (*dharma*) consisting in the absence of subject-status is precisely enjoined therein. (82.7) In the second case, what has happened to the non-entity?

Because, elsewhere, the absence of subjecthood (*dharmitva*) is established [only] for things other than that. However, the third position is entirely redundant because it lacks a basis; thus, how can there be a negation of subjecthood for a non-entity?

Therefore, just as the presentation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is pervaded by the prior acceptance of the state of being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*), [so too is the case here].

Alternatively, the presentation of a denoting word is pervaded by the prior acceptance of a denoted object; likewise, the presentation of the statement "a non-entity lacks the status of being a subject" is pervaded by the prior acceptance of the status of being a subject for a non-entity. Otherwise, the presentation of that statement would be purposeless.

(82.11) Therefore, if the presentation of a statement is the pervaded property (*vyāpyadharma*), then the acceptance of a non-entity as the subject (*dharmin*) would also unavoidably entail the pervading property (*vyāpakadharma*). If, on the other hand, it is not the pervading property, then the presentation of the statement—which is the pervaded—would be impossible; thus, silence would be forced upon you here. How, then, is the contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanapratirodha*) not established?
(82.15) As the Teacher said: "For one who does not speak is not able to awaken another; yet one who speaks cannot avoid this fault. Thus, one enters into a great dilemma.
(82.17) If it is argued that "in a discussion concerning a non-entity, it is only fitting for those with aesthetic sensitivity to remain silent," oh,

what great cleverness! Having himself leaped about as best he could during the discussion of a non-entity and being defeated, he now wishes to escape under the pretext that silence is the logical course.
Furthermore, a discussion concerning a non-entity cannot be prevented merely by royal punishment or by undesirable consequences such as the crushing of one's feet;

for even in this case, when the presence of succession and simultaneity is the probans and the absence of existence is the probandum, who can deny the status of being the subject (*dharmin*) to that which is momentary—whether it be of a nature whose entity-status is doubtful or of a non-entity?
For indeed, three kinds of properties (*dharma*) are observed.
Some [objects] are restricted to real entities, such as blue and so forth; some are restricted to non-entities, such as the absence of all designations;
and some are common to both, such as mere non-apprehension.

In this regard, it is logical that the status of being a subject (dharmin) for a non-entity is negated by means of a property of an entity; however, it is not [negated] by means of a property of a non-entity,
nor by means of a property common to both entity and non-entity.

Because it would follow that one’s own statement could not be introduced, even if there were doubt regarding the non-existence of the non-momentary, its status as a subject (*dharmin*) by means of a property of a non-entity (*avastudharma*) remains unimpeded; thus, this non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) is not "unestablished in its locus" (*āśrayāsiddha*).

It was rightly said that the reason is "unestablished in its locus" when the non-momentary is not cognized, because if that [non-momentary] is not cognized, the conventional usage of it is impossible.
This cognition, which serves as a factor in conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), is not of a single nature regarding both real and unreal entities.
For a cognition of a real entity arises either directly or through a succession of causes from the causal capacity (*sāmarthya*) of that entity—
such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that follows upon direct perception.
But since a non-entity lacks causal efficacy, cognition of it is merely conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*).
For the cognition of a real entity arises through the force of the entity itself: either directly as perception, or indirectly as the conceptual construction following in its wake and as inference.

For that which is a non-entity, there can be no cognition arising from the power of a real entity, because that would entail the loss of its status as a non-entity due to its being a producer [of such a cognition].
Therefore, the cognition of a non-entity is merely conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*).

Indeed, negation (*abhāva*) is not some thing possessing a physical form that must be directly perceived, but rather something that must be dealt with through conventional discourse (*vyavahartavya*).
And that conventional usage is indeed established even from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*);
otherwise, there would be no conventionally recognized usage regarding non-entities, yet such usage is accepted.

(83.6) Since the negation of its being a subject (*dharmin*) follows [from the argument], one must—even if unwillingly—accept that the non-momentary is established by mere conceptual construction. Thus, this reason is not "unestablished in its locus" (*āśrayāsiddha*) on account of being unperceived.
It must be said:
consequently, regarding the claim that for a non-momentary entity established by mere conceptual construction,
"no reason is without a substratum, because a subject established by mere conceptual construction is easily found everywhere," [that argument is undermined].
(83.10) That is incorrect.

For even if a subject established merely through conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*) were possible in all cases, it cannot function as a subject by virtue of being a real property (*vastudharma*).
This is because a reason that depends on a real property as its logical ground can also occur as one whose locus is unestablished (*āśrayāsiddha*).

(83.11) Just as the proof "because its qualities are perceived everywhere" was presented for the purpose of establishing the omnipresence of the self (*ātman*), this presentation of a reason constitutes a conceptual alternative (*vikalpa*);
previously, it was one whose object was doubtful.
But once the reason has been established, we say that it is "without a real entity" (*avastuka*).
Furthermore, the fault of the reason known as "having a doubtful locus" (*sandigdhāśrayatva*) does not apply here;
let that matter rest for now.
For even a doubtful object, though non-existent, is established as a subject (*dharmin*) in relation to its own non-substantial properties (*avastudharma*),
since it is only in relation to a reason that is a property of a real entity (*vastudharma*) that a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) with a doubtful locus (*sandigdhāśraya*) is defined—
as, for example, "there is a peacock in this thicket because of its cry."
The non-existence of the object of a conceptualization that lacks a real substrate has already been established precisely through the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*).
Likewise, it should be understood that even for an example such as a sky-lotus, its status as a subject (*dharmin*) and its cognition through mere conceptualization are to be accepted.

Thus, since it is impossible to deny that a non-entity can function as a subject with respect to its own non-substantial properties, and since its cognition occurs through mere conceptualization, this reason is not one whose locus is unestablished (*āśrayāsiddha*).
Nor is there any damage to the illustrative example,
nor is this [reason] unestablished in its own nature;
for in a non-momentary subject, the two pervaders— succession and simultaneity— are impossible.

For instance, if it possessed the capacity to produce effects occurring in the second and subsequent moments at its first moment, then it would produce the effect belonging to the second and subsequent moments just like the effect belonging to the first moment;
for it is impossible for that which is capable to delay [its action].
(83.22) Now, at that time, there is no capacity characterized by the completeness of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*),
because there is the possibility of incapacity characterized by their deficiency.
For an entity does not act by its own nature alone simply because it acts by its own nature.

If it is argued that "the production of the effect is observed only from that [cause] when accompanied by auxiliary factors," then, for as long as these [factors], being combined, produce the effect, let them possess this "auxiliary character" (*sahakāritva*) defined as the performance of a single purpose; who would deny this? But how is it established that the effect must necessarily be produced by those [factors] alone when combined?
Because an entity possesses a single intrinsic nature throughout its prior and posterior moments,
it is impossible to avoid the unavoidable consequence that it must be restricted to either always producing or never producing.
Therefore, the claim that "the causal complex is the producer, not a single [cause] is the producer" lies beyond the reach of even the daydreams of those who maintain the doctrine of permanence.

(83.29) If it is argued, "What can we do? It is simply seen to be so," let it be seen; however, this is the point of dispute: whether the production of an effect arises from the very same entity that previously existed and subsequently entered into the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), or rather from a different moment produced by that specific causal complex.

In that case, since [the cause] exists even previously, the effect would either arise at all times or never at all; thus, without resolving this contradiction, one who proceeds merely to restate the thesis—that "that very thing" is the production of the effect—deserves pity. Furthermore, identity is not established by recognition alone.
This is because human effort [is seen to be] ineffective in cases such as hair that has been cut and grown back again, or a blade of *kuśa* grass, or the trunk of a plantain tree;
furthermore, we have demonstrated in detail the refutation of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) in our *Sthirasiddhidūṣaṇa*, so that very [work] should be consulted.
[Objection: But surely it is the effect itself that requires auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).
But it is not the cause for the production of the effect.

If it is argued: "Because capacity is twofold—innate and adventitious—and since there is a plurality of auxiliary factors, even for that which is non-momentary, there can be a plurality of effects in succession due to the succession of various auxiliaries," [we reply: no.

(84.8) Let it be granted for now that capacity is twofold, by way of the distinction between innate and adventitious; nevertheless, that particular real entity (*vastu-svalakṣaṇa*), which possesses the property of immediate causal efficiency (*kriyā-dharmaka*), must necessarily be admitted [to exist].
If that [capacity] exists even prior [to the effect],...
If [the cause were permanent], there would be the consequence of the effect being produced even earlier;
if, on the other hand, it produces only later, then the entity is not stable.
(84.11) Nor is it logical that an effect should depend upon auxiliary causes,
because it [the effect] is non-existent.
Furthermore, if a cause, despite being present, does not produce its own effect, [it would follow that it is not a cause].
In that case, it would not be that very effect at all, because of its independence. And as it has been said: "For that which has the nature of producing a subsequent effect..."
How could it perform an action at the outset? In that case, it would not have the inherent nature (svabhāva) of performing that action;
for that which has the inherent nature of producing blue does not also produce yellow and so forth.
(84.15) That is inconsistent. If an entity possesses a stable nature, why is it that this [effect] exists only at a later time and not at an earlier time?
And in the absence of that [time distinction], how can it be said that the cause also possesses the nature of a later effect?
(84.17) What can we do? If you argue that its birth occurs only at a later time, then since that is impossible for something stable, it must indicate instability.
If you argue that even though it is stable, this is simply its nature—that it produces an effect only at a subsequent moment—then [we reply]: [this is untenable].
No; because it is impossible to accept an intrinsic nature that is contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), a non-momentary entity cannot first of all produce effects sequentially.
Nor is the production of non-sequential effects possible;
for if its causal nature were to persist in the second moment as well, it would follow that it must produce the effect once again.

(84.21) If it is argued that once the effect has been produced, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is deficient because its operation upon that object has ceased, and thus it cannot produce what has already been produced—[we reply:

no. For it was already established previously that whether a causal complex is possible or impossible, its capacity to produce must be determined based on the presence of the essential nature of the action and the factors of action (*kāraka*) at that very moment.
Indeed, the fact that the effect has already been produced makes it impossible to produce again; this very impossibility indicates that the cause is incapable [of further production].
(84.23) Therefore, this absence of the capacity to produce effects either successively or simultaneously in the case of a non-momentary entity is not unestablished.

Nor is there the possibility of any other mode besides succession and simultaneity, such that—were it not pervaded by those two—the reason would have a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatireka*).
For if one were to suspect another mode, even after refuting both modes of visibility and invisibility, it would follow that one could have no confidence in one's own position as well.

Therefore, no other mode of existence is possible than the establishment of mutual exclusion; for neither a real entity nor a non-entity that does not enter into its own nature can possess a nature other than that [of itself],
since any other mode would likewise fail to enter into the nature of the sequence.

Likewise, even though the auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*) is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), the pervasion of existence (*sattva*)—conjoined with a perceptible auxiliary—by means of succession and simultaneity is established through perception alone by way of excluding non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*).

Thus, the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is pervaded by succession and simultaneity; since these two are established as mutually exclusive, the meaning is that the capacity for causal efficiency does not go elsewhere, having been excluded from these two modes.
Therefore, upon the cessation of these two, [the probandum] ceases as well.
(85.4) Regarding Trilocana’s threefold conceptualization, the first objection has been refuted by avoiding the fault of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
The second, moreover, is irrelevant. (85.5)
Because the absence [of the object] is cognized through conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*);
for non-existence is not some entity possessing a physical form that must be directly perceived,
but rather it is to be dealt with through conceptualization alone.
For there is no apprehension or non-apprehension of a non-entity other than through conceptual construction (vikalpa) in any way whatsoever;
for in either case, it would follow that the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding it would be lost.
Thus, the apprehension of the example of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*) and the exclusion of the reason (*hetuvyatireka*) occurs precisely through conceptual construction.
(85.9) The third objection, too, is irrelevant;
for the pervasion of existence by momentariness remains unimpeded by the faultless non-perception of the pervader.
(85.11) Thus, this non-perception of the pervader [establishes] the non-existence of the non-momentary.
Therefore, it is established that [the argument] proves the exclusion of the self from the entity and its pervasion by momentariness because it consists of a single operation.
Now, if "non-perception of the pervader" (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) refers merely to non-perception, then it cannot produce the cognition of the probandum because it is a non-entity.
Nor can "perception of something else" be called "non-perception of the pervader," since there is no perception of anything else, such as a bare ground, etc. If this is argued:
(85.15) That is incorrect,
because non-perception elsewhere is established precisely through the perception of the locus (*dharmin*).

For instance, in the case of "there is no *śiṃśapā* here because of the absence of trees," the perception of the locus— the bare spot— in relation to the tree constitutes the non-perception of the tree.

Furthermore, with respect to a *śiṃśapā* tree, the very perception of the locus (*dharmin*) as a bare space is itself the perception of the absence of the *śiṃśapā*; thus, the operation of the "non-perception of the pervader" (*vyāpakānupalambha*) results in the establishment of a "reason based on essential nature" (*svabhāvahetu*).

Likewise, with respect to a permanent locus determined by conceptual cognition, the non-perception of successive or non-successive activity occurs simply through the apprehension of it as a bare [locus] when viewed in relation to such activities.

Moreover, with respect to causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), the mere cognition of the bare [locus] is itself the cognition of the connection with causal efficiency; therefore, there is no distinction whatsoever between this and another instance of the "non-perception of the pervader."

(85.22) Furthermore, with respect to determination (*adhyavasāya*), there is the conventional usage of establishing the absence of the pervaded due to the absence of the pervader in an external, non-momentary entity. And this determination should be understood as the capacity to engage [with an object] even when it is not actually grasped, owing to its connection with a specific form that has arisen through the power of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). Such a determination has been established in our *Citrādvaitasiddhi*.
And that non-contradictory conventional practice cannot be avoided;
for by this sequence as well, the very same point is established: "that which is devoid of the pervader is devoid of the pervaded."
And this principle applies just as it does when the subject (*dharmin*) is a real entity, so too when it is not a real entity; what difference is there?
For in this case, that which is associated with a single cognition is merely conceptualized (*vikalpita*);
just as, for example, a horn associated with a single cognition was perceived by him on the head of a deer.
Even in the case of the rabbit’s head, the horn is negated precisely through the possibility of its association with a single cognition together with that [head].

Likewise, in the case of blue and so forth, where the status of being eternal or non-eternal is not yet determined, succession and simultaneity are seen to be associated with a single cognition along with their own substratum (*svadharmin*).

If they were to exist in an eternal entity, they would be apprehended by the cognition grasping the eternal exactly together with that eternal substratum; it is through this possibility—namely, by way of association with a single cognition—that they are negated.

But how is it that succession and non-succession do not manifest within this eternal cognition, given that one conceptualizes the eternal precisely as being encompassed by succession and non-succession? For this very reason, the introduction of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) is possible, because such an argument would otherwise be futile without the presence of a contrary superimposition (*viparītāropa*).
Eternality consists in having a single nature even at different times, whereas succession and non-succession consist in having different natures across two moments.

Therefore, since permanence and the capacity for successive or simultaneous causal efficiency are characterized by mutual exclusion, their contradiction is unavoidable; how, then, can succession and simultaneity be subsumed within the permanent? And because they are not so subsumed, how can there be any conceptual representation [of the permanent] by a conceptual construction of the "purely permanent" that has cast away the superimposition of succession and simultaneity? Consequently, even when the counter-correlate—the permanent—is being conceptually constructed...

In a case where [the object] has attained the characteristic of being associated with a single cognition, there is indeed the constant non-perception of succession and simultaneity— which are constantly contradicted by that perception— and from that very fact, there is the non-perception of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāśakti*). Therefore, because it consists in the perception of a subject (*dharmin*) that is devoid of the pervader (*vyāpaka*),
it does not differ from other types of non-perception of the pervader.

(86.13) [Objection: But surely this is useful because it has as its basis a real entity (*vastu*) that possesses the property of being non-existent; for the establishment of valid cognition (*pramāṇavyavasthā*) is based upon a real entity. [Reply: What is this so-called "having a real entity as its basis"? Does it mean that [the cognition] originates from a real entity even through a mediated succession, or rather that it is the cause for linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) regarding a real entity in some particular form?

Or [it is] being dependent upon a real entity (*vastubhūta*) as its subject (*dharmin*). (86.16) If the first position is held, then this [dependence] is likewise not exhausted, for it too is dependent upon a real entity that is the object of the apprehension of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between succession and simultaneity and causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Nor is there any fault possible in the second position either, because this [pervasion] is the means for proving an entity characterized by momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgin*).

Nor can even the final alternative be conceived. This is because that very entity which is the subject (*dharmin*) of the conceptualization of permanence is established as being devoid of external permanent substrata— just like [the absence of] causal efficiency characterized by succession and non-succession—

and because it is possible for [the reason] to be connected to a subject that is a real entity in the form of a non-momentary nature belonging to the intellect, by way of a relative negation (*paryudāsa*).

(86.23) This very same principle should be applied to such cases as "the speaker is not the son of a barren woman because he lacks consciousness," and so forth. By this, Trilocana—who claimed that while [negations] such as the absence of a tree can be subsumed [within the categories of non-existence], this [absence of sequence, etc. cannot—is also refuted. (86.25) Furthermore, the absence of sequence and so forth does not transcend the three classes of fallacies.

Even if [the property] is a property of non-existence (*abhāvadharmatva*), this is because the fault of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) has been avoided. (86.26) As for what was stated by him—that when the non-existence of eternal things is established through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the fact that they lack succession and so forth is established as a property of non-existence—that is difficult to maintain even for a child. For "eternal" is the subject (*dharmin*). "Non-existence" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*). [The probans is] the absence of being a producer of successive effects or a producer of non-successive effects.

This is the reason (*hetu*). Its being a property of non-existence (*abhāvadharmatva*) is said to mean its inseparable connection (*avinābhāvitva*) with the probandum (*sādhya*), which is characterized by non-existence. And since the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of existence by succession and simultaneity has been established, the absence of the pervader—succession and simultaneity—is established by the absence of the pervaded—existence; thus, its being a property of non-existence is established even prior to the proof of the pervasion between the two positive entities.
It is established by either perception, inference, or another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus, there is no fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

Nor is the same consequence applicable to non-existence as it is to existence, because the principles (*nyāya*) involved are different. For in that case, both the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) are real entities (*vastu*), and their locus (*dharmin*) is likewise a real entity.
The establishment of a real entity occurs only through perception and inference; in the absence of these two, there is necessarily a failure to establish the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).

This is correct. However, in the case of proving non-existence (*asattā*), a reason that is a property of a non-entity (*avastudharma*) can be refuted by the fault of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), since the subject (*dharmin*) is established merely through conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*). Likewise, the contradiction of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) for a non-momentary entity through either succession or simultaneity is indeed established.
Thus, by conceptual construction alone, the non-momentary is established as the contradictory [of causal efficiency]. And its nature is that which is delineated by conceptual construction.

One must also employ the expression "not another. Otherwise, when negations such as "being devoid of succession and non-succession" are stated by way of referring back to that [non-existent thing], since its own nature is not indicated but something else is indicated, there would follow the absurd consequence that words such as "non-momentary" or "the horn of a hare" could not be uttered.

Yet they do exist. Therefore, just as the negation of beauty and so forth is applied to the son of a barren woman and the like—which are established through conceptual construction even in the absence of a means of valid cognition—[so too is the case here].

Likewise, what fault could there be in establishing a contradiction between that very non-momentary form— which is brought forth by conceptual construction— and its opposite? If, on the other hand, the negation of contradiction is due to the absence of experience of the non-momentary, then let there likewise be no negation of beauty and so forth based on the experience of the son of a barren woman.

(87.20) [Objection: But if this is so, then contradiction (*virodha*) would be non-ultimate (*apāramārthika*). Consequently, the proof of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) by means of that [contradiction] would also be non-ultimate. [Reply: We do not maintain, nor is it logically tenable, that contradiction is some distinct entity (*vastvantara*) designated as a relation whose "feet" are placed upon both poles [of the contradictories]. For if that were the case, it might be non-ultimate in the absence of reality in one of the related entities. However, in accordance with how it is actually maintained [by us], it is indeed ultimate (*pāramārthika*).
The meaning of contradiction between two things considered to be opposed is merely their mutual exclusion of each other's essential nature (*svarūpa*).
And this [contradiction] exists only in an ultimate sense (*pāramārthika*) regarding existence and non-existence;
existence does not enter into the form of non-existence.
Nor does non-existence enter into the nature of existence; this very rule of their non-confusion is what constitutes ultimate contradiction.
For permanence consists in having a single form throughout different times, whereas succession and simultaneity consist in having distinct forms even within two moments.
Therefore, there is indeed a contradiction between permanence and the capacity to produce effects either successively or simultaneously, just as there is between existence and non-existence.

(88.1) If it is objected: "But surely, apart from the contradictory properties of permanence and being characterized by succession or simultaneity, there is no such thing as contradiction; so what could possibly possess reality?"
(88.2) No, for we do not assert that contradiction is ultimately real by virtue of the existence of a separate entity [called "contradiction"].
Rather, it exists when two contradictory properties are present.
Otherwise, even if there were a separate entity named "contradiction," if the two properties themselves were not contradictory, how could there be the possibility of an ultimate contradiction?
If two properties are contradictory, the conventional usage of "contradiction" is established by that alone;
what is the use of another distinct entity called "contradiction," which is established merely by a verbal proposition?
(88.7) This, then, is the summary of the prima facie position.

"An eternal [entity] does not exist, nor is it an object of cognition; therefore, the reason [you provide] suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*). Furthermore, your own experience is undermined, and even the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is discarded. Moreover, emptiness is not established by either [of these two]. Nor is non-existence established in the same way that existence is not [established] through an eternal [entity]; for it is impossible to establish a contradiction with a non-existent thing, such as succession and so forth. (88.12) Herein lies the summary of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*).
Is there, or is there not, in this world any practice of negation or affirmation regarding some property that is established by the mind with respect to a non-entity?
If it exists somewhere, how can there not be so many refutations? If it does not exist at all, then the contradiction of one's own words is established.
Therefore, the ultimate truth is this: a permanent entity is not capable of performing successive effects, nor is it capable of performing simultaneous effects.
Consequently, the ultimate truth is that even that which is endowed with existence is not [non-momentary] at all.

Furthermore, since there is no other category apart from the momentary and the non-momentary, this existence—which is excluded from the non-momentary—is established as being pervaded by the momentary alone as its point of rest. Thus, the proof of momentariness from existence is free from contradiction.
(88.21) Since liberation is held to arise from the awakening to the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) of all phenomena,
that very momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), which crushes the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*), has been established here. (88.23) Thus ends this work by Ratnakīrti.
